candidate.stem: Suppose compute-based scaling laws keep holding for the next few decades. How much uncertainty would remain about when transformative AI (TAI) arrives, and why?

options.text: A lot: the laws tie compute to performance, but not to how much compute TAI needs, and estimates of that span many orders of magnitude
Little: once compute is tied to performance, arrival follows from compute trends, which are tracked closely enough to name a year
options.provenance: misreads 'Even if we assume compute-based scaling laws hold, we still don't know how much compute TAI will actually require' as saying the laws settle the timing

options.text: A lot: the compute TAI needs is pegged to the human brain, and direct measurements of the brain's compute are still too noisy to pin down
options.provenance: misreads the source of the biological-anchors spread as measurement error, when the section attributes it to which biological process is taken as the reference (lifetime learning vs evolutionary history)

options.text: Some, but a bounded amount: errors in the compute trend stay about the same size however far ahead the forecast is run
options.provenance: misses 'compound over time' in the lead 'All forecasts come with wide error margins that compound over time'

candidate.explanation: Scaling laws tell you how performance rises with compute. They don't tell you where on that curve transformative AI sits, and that is the quantity people disagree about. Biological-anchor estimates of the compute TAI requires run from what a human uses learning skills over a lifetime to everything evolution spent shaping humans, which is roughly twelve orders of magnitude. The spread comes from choosing which biological process to treat as the reference, not from noisy brain measurements, so better neuroscience instruments wouldn't close it. The 'little' option assumes that fixing the curve fixes the target. The 'bounded' option misses that errors compound: a small miss in a yearly growth rate grows with every year the projection runs. That's why a date like '2045' should be read as the rough centre of a wide range. (Forecasting Timelines)
candidate.takeaway: Scaling laws give you the curve, not the finish line; the uncertainty about how much compute TAI needs survives even if the laws hold perfectly.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: 'even if scaling laws hold we don't know how much compute TAI requires, and anchors span orders of magnitude' is a sentence a reader of the section can produce unaided.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick either 'A lot' option by the section's obvious uncertainty theme, but the noisy-measurement option also says 'A lot' and names the brain, so the choice turns on knowing the spread comes from the reference process; 'TAI' and 'compute' appear in several options, so they are not a word-match tell.
